description: DeepSonic explores Earth science beyond visualization by transforming depth data into meaningful, interactive sound. Our idea combines satellite imagery, data analysis, machine learning, and real-time sonification to convert variations in underwater depth into an engaging auditory experience, helping people discover and understand the hidden underwater world through both sight and sound.
summary:
DEEPSONIC is an exploratory ocean-data sonification project developed for NASA Space Apps Challenge’s The Earth Jukebox challenge. It transforms satellite-derived ocean-colour reflectance data into musical sounds, offering a new way to experience and explore our oceans.
The project uses NASA’s PACE-OCI satellite data and converts four selected reflectance bands into musical frequencies, assigning each band a different instrument: piano, flute, marimba and violin. It also incorporates ICESat-2 ATL24 bathymetry observations and NASA sea-surface temperature data for spatial comparison,analysis and validation of results from reflectance data.
By combining satellite imagery, scientific data visualisation and sound, DEEPSONIC makes complex Earth observations more interactive and accessible. Its goal is to explore how listening to satellite data can complement traditional maps and graphs, encourage scientific curiosity, and create a more engaging connection with our oceans.
details:
DEEPSONIC is an interactive Python-based workflow that allows users to select an ocean region and transform its satellite-derived reflectance data into sound.

Working:

  1. Select an area: The user draws an Area of Interest (AOI) on an interactive map. The selected boundary is exported as GeoJSON for spatial processing.
  2. Retrieve NASA data: Using NASA Earthdata authentication, the notebook searches for and retrieves PACE-OCI Level-2 Apparent Optical Properties data.
  3. Process ocean-colour data: Four remote-sensing reflectance bands-Rrs443, Rrs482, Rrs561 and Rrs655 are extracted and processed.
  4. Create music: The reflectance values are normalised and mapped to audible frequencies between 220 and 880 Hz. Each band is assigned a musical instrument: piano, flute, marimba or violin. These sounds are synthesised into a four-instrument WAV composition.
  5. Compare and analyse: The project also retrieves ICESat-2 ATL24 bathymetry observations and NASA MUR sea-surface temperature data. Spatial matching and correlation analysis are used to explore relationships between ocean-colour reflectance and water depth.
  6. Generate outputs: The notebook produces audio, maps, plots and a CSV comparison file.

Benefits and impact:

DEEPSONIC introduces sound as an alternative way to explore satellite observations. It can help people experience variations in ocean-colour data beyond conventional maps, graphs and numerical tables. The project also brings together multiple NASA Earth-observation datasets in one workflow, creating opportunities for further exploration of ocean science, remote sensing and data sonification.

Its intended impact is to make Earth science more engaging and accessible, encourage interdisciplinary learning, and demonstrate how scientific datasets can be transformed into creative experiences.

Also rather than relying on BATHYMETRY assumed formulae we can get the shallow water depth information directly from reflectance data.

Tools and technologies used:

  • Programming language: Python
  • Development environment: Google Colab Platform
  • NASA data access: NASA Earthdata and the earthaccess library
  • Geospatial processing: GeoPandas, Shapely and ipyleaflet
  • Data formats and processing: NetCDF4 and Python scientific/geospatial processing tools
  • Satellite datasets: NASA PACE-OCI, ICESat-2 ATL24 and NASA MUR Sea Surface Temperature
  • Outputs: WAV audio, CSV data, interactive maps and scientific visualisations

Creativity:

The creative aspect of DEEPSONIC lies in translating numerical ocean-colour observations into musical notes. Instead of viewing four reflectance bands only as values or colour patterns, the project gives each band a distinct musical identity. This creates an auditory interpretation of satellite data and connects science with music and technology.

Factors and current limitations:

The workflow considers the selected geographic area, availability and quality of satellite observations, spatial matching distance, missing data and the relationship between different datasets. In the current comparison, 53 PACE pixels were matched with ATL24 bathymetry observations within a maximum distance of 150 metres. The results are exploratory and do not yet establish a validated method for predicting water depth from reflectance. Further testing across different regions and acquisition dates, along with more extensive validation, is needed.

DEEPSONIC is therefore intended as a creative scientific exploration and a foundation for further research not a replacement for established bathymetric measurement methods.
